The Bigmouth flounder, Hippoglossina stomata, exhibits a maximum recorded total length of 40 cm [Li = 40 cm] for females, a size reached only after several years of sustained somatic growth in the productive waters of the eastern Pacific. This length corresponds to an ultimate wet body mass of approximately 784 grams [Wwi = approximately 784 grams] when applying a length-weight relationship derived from this family, reflecting the substantial culmination of tissue accretion over the fish's lifetime. Upon eclosion from the pelagic egg, the newly emerged yolk-sac larva carries a tiny initial endowment, with a hatchling wet weight of roughly 0.00022 grams [Wwb = roughly 0.00022 grams]. This minuscule starting mass, typical of flatfishes producing numerous small pelagic eggs, necessitates a rapid onset of exogenous feeding to fuel the subsequent growth trajectory. Understanding these fundamental size benchmarks is critical for parameterizing the life history of this little-studied paralichthyid, as they set the energetic stage for all later developmental transitions, from the pelagic larval phase through benthic settlement and eventual sexual maturation.

Females of Hippoglossina stomata reach the onset of gonadal activation and reproductive maturity at a total length of 16.2 cm [Lp = 16.2 cm], a size that is attained well before the ultimate length of 40 cm. The corresponding wet body mass at this pubertal milestone is estimated at 48.5 grams [Wwp = 48.5 grams], representing only about six percent of the ultimate wet weight of 784 grams. This decoupling between the size at which ovarian development commences and the final asymptotic mass is a common pattern among iteroparous flatfishes, indicating that a considerable fraction of the adult lifespan is spent investing in both continued somatic expansion and reproductive effort. The pubertal length is particularly important for stock assessment, as it directly determines the size at which females first contribute to the spawning biomass. Field surveys and otolith-based back-calculations suggest that individuals generally achieve this length within their second or third year, although local environmental conditions and food availability can influence the precise timing of this developmental milestone.

Under controlled laboratory conditions designed to reflect the thermal regime of their native habitat at 17.1 °C [T = 17.1 °C], the maximum reproductive output of female Bigmouth flounder has been characterized. Their spawning activity is best described not as a frantic daily production of eggs, but rather as a seasonal process involving discrete clutches. Field data, supplemented by comparative studies on the related Pacific sanddab Citharichthys sordidus, indicate that females produce approximately 60 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 60 eggs per clutch] and may initiate a new clutch roughly once every day during the peak of the spawning season [F_R_i = spawning season]. This reproductive strategy, which yields a substantial cumulative fecundity over the spawning period, allows the species to exploit favorable oceanographic conditions for larval survival. The 17.1 °C temperature is significant because it approximates the thermal optimum for oocyte development and vitellogenesis, as deviations from this temperature have been shown to reduce clutch frequency and egg viability in related paralichthyid flatfishes.

The lifespan of Bigmouth flounder in the wild, based on mark-recapture studies and validated otolith age readings, reaches a maximum of approximately 9 years [am = approximately 9 years] when the population is experiencing the average thermal conditions of their range, which typically center around 17.1 °C [T = 17.1 °C]. This longevity places the species in an intermediate position among eastern Pacific flatfishes; some small-bodied species live only 3 to 5 years, while larger halibuts can exceed 20 years. The 9-year maximum age implies a generational turnover that is slow enough to make the population vulnerable to sustained fishing pressure, yet rapid enough to allow for considerable inter-annual variability in recruitment success. This lifespan, combined with the iteroparous reproductive strategy, means that a single female can participate in multiple spawning seasons, potentially producing well over sixty eggs in each clutch [N_R_i = sixty eggs in each clutch] in each successive year. The sustained energetic demands of this extended reproductive window highlight the importance of adequate prey resources throughout adult life.

The morphological transformation from pelagic larva to benthic juvenile in Hippoglossina stomata involves a pronounced leftward migration of the eye, a classic pleuronectiform trait that precedes settlement. During this metamorphic climax, the transparent, bilaterally symmetrical larva begins to assume the asymmetrical body plan of the adult, a process that is energetically demanding and typically completed within a few weeks at 17.1 °C [T = 17.1 °C]. Following settlement, the post-metamorphic juveniles recruit to soft-bottom habitats, where they feed predominantly on small crustaceans and polychaetes. The growth rate during this juvenile phase is rapid, allowing the fish to achieve the pubertal total length of 16.2 cm [Lp = 16.2 cm] and its corresponding mass of 48.5 grams [Wwp = 48.5 grams] within a relatively short timeframe. However, the progression from that point to the asymptotic length of 40 cm [Li = 40 cm] decelerates markedly, with the maximum body size approached only as the fish nears its recorded longevity of 9 years [am = 9 years] — a pattern typical of flatfishes that partition energy between early reproductive output and continued somatic gain at a temperature of 17.1 °C [T = 17.1 °C].
